title: Accidentally Drank on Metronidazole? What to Do Right Now
excerpt: Had a drink while taking metronidazole (Flagyl)? A calm, step-by-step plan: what to do right now, which symptoms are normal, the ER red flags, and why you shouldn't skip your next dose.
metaDescription: Accidentally drank alcohol on metronidazole (Flagyl)? What to do now, symptoms to watch for, ER red flags, and why you shouldn't skip your next dose.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** if you accidentally drank alcohol while taking metronidazole (Flagyl), you will most likely be okay. Many people who do this feel nothing unusual at all, and when a reaction does happen it is usually a few hours of flushing, headache, nausea, or a pounding heart that passes on its own. The things that matter now are simple: stop drinking, don't skip your next dose, watch how you feel for the next few hours, and call your pharmacist if you're unsure. Get emergency care right away if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or vomiting you can't stop.

**The quick steps:** Put the drink down and don't have any more. Drink water and sit or lie somewhere comfortable. Take your next metronidazole dose at its normal time unless a doctor or pharmacist tells you otherwise. Don't drive. Call your pharmacist or, in the US, Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** if you want advice on your specific situation. They take calls about drug interactions, not only poisonings, and the call is free. Then go back to avoiding alcohol until at least 72 hours after your last pill.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the official label guidance for metronidazole. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and why you were prescribed the drug. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist** about any alcohol you've had during treatment, especially if you are pregnant, have a heart condition, or also take warfarin or another blood thinner, lithium, or disulfiram (Antabuse). **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** you develop chest pain or tightness, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, trouble breathing, fainting or near-fainting, confusion, a severe headache that is getting worse, or vomiting that won't stop or contains blood.

## What Happens If You Drink on Metronidazole?

Metronidazole is an antibiotic and anti-parasite medicine prescribed for common infections such as bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, some dental infections, certain gut infections, and giardia. Its US prescribing information tells people to avoid alcohol while taking it and for at least three days afterward, because the combination has been associated with what the label calls a **"disulfiram-like reaction."**

Here's what that means in plain words. When you drink, your liver turns alcohol into a toxic chemical called **acetaldehyde**, and then an enzyme called aldehyde dehydrogenase quickly turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate. Disulfiram (Antabuse), a drug used to discourage drinking, blocks that second step. Acetaldehyde builds up and the person gets hot, red, sick, and shaky. For decades it was assumed metronidazole did the same thing, which is where the warning came from.

The science behind that assumption is weaker than most people realize. A small placebo-controlled study in healthy volunteers (Visapää and colleagues, *Annals of Pharmacotherapy*, 2002) found no rise in acetaldehyde and no classic reaction when people drank after taking metronidazole. A review of the published case reports in the same journal (Williams and Woodcock, 2000) concluded that the evidence for a true disulfiram-like interaction was thin. At the same time, case reports of people getting flushing, vomiting, and a racing heart after drinking on metronidazole do exist, and nobody can predict who will react. That is why the warning stays on the label. We cover the full debate in our main [metronidazole and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol).

For someone who has already had a drink, that research is actually reassuring. It suggests a serious reaction is uncommon, and that many people will notice little or nothing. It does not mean you can keep drinking, and it does not mean you should ignore symptoms if they show up.

### Why you might feel sick anyway

Even without any special reaction, there are three other reasons you might feel rough after drinking on metronidazole:

1. **The drug itself.** Nausea, a metallic taste, headache, and stomach upset are common side effects of metronidazole whether or not you drink.
2. **The infection.** Your body is fighting something, and that alone can leave you tired and queasy.
3. **The alcohol.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, dehydrates you, and disrupts sleep. Add it to the first two and you can feel much worse than you'd expect from the amount you drank.

So if you feel a bit off, it doesn't automatically mean you're having a dangerous reaction. What matters is how strong the symptoms are and which ones they are.

## What to Do Right Now: A Step-by-Step Plan

Work through these in order. Most people only need the first four.

### 1. Stop drinking

This sounds obvious, but it's the step people skip. "I've already had one, so I might as well finish the night" is how a mild, unnoticed exposure turns into a rough one. If there is any reaction, more alcohol makes it stronger. Switch to water, soda water, or a soft drink.

### 2. Get comfortable and hydrate

Sit or lie down somewhere cool. Sip water steadily rather than gulping a large amount at once, which can trigger nausea. If you feel sick, small sips of an electrolyte drink or plain water are easier to keep down. A light snack such as toast or crackers can help settle your stomach if you can tolerate it.

### 3. Don't drive, and don't be alone if you feel unwell

Alcohol plus a possible reaction (dizziness, a drop in blood pressure, feeling faint) is a bad mix behind the wheel. If you're feeling symptoms, tell someone nearby what happened so they can keep an eye on you and call for help if things get worse.

### 4. Watch for symptoms over the next few hours

Reactions linked to alcohol and this type of drug tend to start fairly soon after drinking, often within minutes to an hour or so, and they usually fade over several hours. If a few hours have passed since your drink and you feel normal, a significant reaction becomes much less likely. Keep an eye on yourself for the rest of the night anyway, and especially if you had more than one drink.

### 5. Take your next dose on schedule

Don't skip a dose to "make room" for the alcohol, and don't stop the course. More on this below, because it's the most common mistake people make.

### 6. Call a pharmacist if you have questions

A pharmacist can tell you, in a two-minute call, whether your dose, your other medicines, and the amount you drank change anything. If your pharmacy is closed, US readers can call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 at any hour. Outside the US, use your local poison information line or a non-emergency medical helpline.

### 7. Restart the 72-hour clock

From this point, avoid alcohol for the rest of your course and for at least 72 hours (three full days) after your final dose. If you had a drink on day three of a seven-day course, the plan doesn't change: finish the course, then wait three days after the last pill.

## Symptoms to Watch For

If a reaction does happen, it tends to look like a stronger version of the flushing some people get from alcohol. The symptoms described on the label and in case reports include:

- A hot, red face, neck, or chest (flushing)
- A throbbing headache
- Nausea and vomiting
- Stomach cramps or abdominal pain
- A fast or pounding heartbeat
- Sweating
- Dizziness or light-headedness
- Feeling short of breath

**Mild and usually manageable at home:** some flushing, a headache, mild nausea, feeling warm, or a heartbeat that's a little faster than normal but steady. These usually settle within a few hours as your body clears the alcohol. If your heart is racing and you want to understand what's normal after drinking, our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains the common causes and the signs that need a check.

**Not mild, needs medical help:** the symptoms in the box below. A dangerous drop in blood pressure and heart rhythm problems have been reported in rare cases, and those are exactly the cases where speed matters.

## When to Go to the ER or Call 911

> **Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if, after drinking on metronidazole, you or someone else has:**
>
> - Chest pain, pressure, or tightness
> - A very fast, irregular, or fluttering heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest
> - Trouble breathing or feeling like you can't get enough air
> - Fainting, nearly fainting, or being too dizzy to stand
> - Confusion, unusual drowsiness, or being hard to wake
> - Vomiting that won't stop, or vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee grounds
> - A severe headache that keeps getting worse
> - Swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or a widespread rash (these can be signs of an allergic reaction to the drug itself)
>
> **Call your doctor or pharmacist the same day if** your symptoms are milder but haven't eased after a few hours, you vomited soon after taking a dose and aren't sure whether to repeat it, or you are pregnant, have a heart condition, or take blood thinners.

If the person drank a lot, also think about alcohol poisoning on its own. Vomiting while confused or very drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, cold or bluish skin, or being unable to wake up are emergencies regardless of any medication. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers what to look for and what to do while you wait for help. Never leave someone who is very drunk and vomiting alone, and lie them on their side.

## Should You Skip Your Next Metronidazole Dose?

No. This is the single most important point on this page.

It's a natural instinct: you've had a drink, you're worried about a reaction, so you think about skipping a pill to give the alcohol time to clear. It's the wrong move, for three reasons:

1. **Skipping doesn't make you safe to drink.** Metronidazole stays in your body for a while after each dose (its half-life, meaning the time it takes for the level in your blood to drop by half, is around eight hours). Missing one pill doesn't clear it from your system.
2. **Skipping weakens the treatment.** Antibiotics work by keeping the drug level high enough, for long enough, to clear the infection. Gaps give the infection a chance to hang on, which can mean the infection comes back and you need another course.
3. **Some of these infections affect other people.** Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection, and incompletely treated infections can be passed on. Finishing the course protects your partners too.

The better plan is the one above: stop drinking now, take your next dose at the usual time, and don't drink again until 72 hours after you finish. If you're worried because you drank a lot, or because your next dose is due very soon after drinking, call your pharmacist and ask. They may tell you to take it as normal, which is the usual advice, but they can check your situation.

### What if I vomited after my dose?

If you threw up soon after taking a pill, some of the dose may have come back up. Don't automatically take another one. Call your pharmacist or the prescriber and tell them how long after the dose you vomited. They will tell you whether to repeat it or just carry on with the next scheduled dose.

## Does Alcohol Make Metronidazole Stop Working?

There is no good evidence that a drink makes metronidazole less effective at killing the bacteria or parasites it targets. The main concern with alcohol and this drug is the possible reaction and the extra side effects, not the antibiotic failing.

That said, alcohol can still get in the way of your recovery indirectly:

- **Vomiting** can mean you lose part of a dose.
- **Skipped doses** (because you felt sick, forgot, or skipped on purpose) are a much bigger threat to the treatment than the alcohol itself.
- **Poor sleep and dehydration** make it harder for your body to fight the infection and can make you feel worse for longer.

So one accidental drink is very unlikely to ruin your treatment. Repeated drinking, missed doses, or a night of vomiting could. If your symptoms from the original infection don't improve by the end of the course, let your doctor know, whatever the reason.

## Different Situations, Different Levels of Worry

People land on this page from a lot of different starting points. Here's how to think about the most common ones.

### "I had one drink"

This is the most common case and usually the least worrying. Stop there, follow the steps above, and keep an eye on yourself for a few hours. If you feel fine, carry on with your course as normal and avoid alcohol from here on.

### "I had several drinks before I remembered"

The more you drink, the stronger any reaction can be, and the more alcohol itself adds nausea, dehydration, and a hangover on top of the drug's side effects. Stop now, don't drink more, hydrate, and don't be alone if you're feeling unwell. A call to a pharmacist or Poison Control is a sensible idea. Watch closely for the emergency signs listed above.

### "I drank, then took my metronidazole dose"

The advice is the same: don't take extra, don't skip the next one, and watch for symptoms. If you feel fine a few hours later, carry on with the course as prescribed.

### "I drank the night before my first dose"

Alcohol from a normal night out is usually mostly cleared by the next day, though after heavy drinking it can take well into the following day. If you still feel drunk or very hungover, it's reasonable to ask your pharmacist whether to start the course a few hours later. Don't delay treatment by days because of it. Once you start, no more alcohol.

### "I drank less than 72 hours after my last pill"

This is a lower-risk situation than drinking mid-course, because the drug level is falling and much of it will have cleared. The 72-hour window is a safety margin, built around how long the drug takes to leave the body, rather than a cliff edge. Stop drinking, watch for the same symptoms, and the chances are you'll be fine.

### "I used mouthwash" or "I took cough syrup"

Many mouthwashes contain alcohol, and some liquid cold and cough medicines do too. NyQuil liquid, for example, has historically contained alcohol, which is one reason our [NyQuil and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol) covers it in detail. The amount you absorb from rinsing and spitting is small, and a reaction from mouthwash alone would be unusual, though the official advice is still to avoid alcohol-containing products during the course and for three days after. Switch to an alcohol-free mouthwash and check the label of any liquid medicine for "alcohol" or "ethanol" before you take more.

### "I ate food cooked with wine" or "I had kombucha"

Cooking burns off some alcohol but not all of it, and kombucha usually contains a small amount. These are small exposures. Don't panic, watch how you feel, and avoid them for the rest of the course if you want to be cautious.

## How to Ease a Mild Reaction at Home

If your symptoms are mild (flushing, headache, mild nausea, feeling warm) and none of the emergency signs are present, these steps can help you feel better while it passes:

- **Rest somewhere cool.** Loosen tight clothing and lie down if you feel dizzy, ideally on your side if you're nauseous.
- **Sip fluids slowly.** Water or a diluted electrolyte drink is best. Avoid caffeine if your heart is racing.
- **Eat something bland when you can.** Toast, crackers, rice, or a banana are gentle on the stomach. Our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more ideas for settling your stomach.
- **Breathe slowly.** A racing heart can feel scary, and anxiety can make it faster. Slow, steady breathing helps you tell whether your heart is settling.
- **Check before you take any other medicine.** Ask a pharmacist before taking anything for the headache or nausea. Some products contain alcohol themselves, and night-time cold and sleep remedies add sedation on top of the alcohol.

### What not to do

- **Don't have more alcohol** to "even out" or to test whether you're reacting.
- **Don't make yourself vomit.** It won't remove alcohol that's already absorbed, and it can lose part of your antibiotic dose.
- **Don't take extra metronidazole** to make up for anything.
- **Don't take sleeping pills or sedating antihistamines** to sleep it off without checking with a pharmacist first.
- **Don't drive** until you feel completely normal and the alcohol has cleared.

## Who Should Call a Doctor Even If They Feel Fine

For most healthy adults, an accidental drink on metronidazole is a "watch and wait" situation. Some people should check in with a doctor or pharmacist even without symptoms:

- **If you're pregnant.** Metronidazole is commonly prescribed in pregnancy for infections such as bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis, and alcohol is best avoided in pregnancy in any case. Let your midwife or doctor know what happened so they can advise you.
- **If you take warfarin or another blood thinner.** Metronidazole's label warns that it can strengthen the effect of warfarin, which raises bleeding risk, and alcohol can affect blood thinners too. Your clinic may want to check your blood test sooner.
- **If you take lithium.** The label notes that metronidazole can raise lithium levels. Alcohol can affect hydration and how your body handles lithium as well.
- **If you take disulfiram (Antabuse)** or have taken it in the last two weeks. Metronidazole's label warns against this combination on its own, and adding alcohol to disulfiram causes a strong reaction. Call your doctor promptly.
- **If you have heart disease, a heart rhythm problem, or low blood pressure.** These are the people for whom a flushing, racing-heart reaction carries the most risk.
- **If you have liver disease.** Your body may clear both the drug and the alcohol more slowly.
- **If you're older or quite unwell from the infection.** Dehydration and drops in blood pressure hit harder.

If you're not sure which other medicines might matter, our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) is a useful starting point, but your pharmacist has your actual list and is the best person to ask.

## What to Tell Your Pharmacist or Doctor

You don't need to feel embarrassed. Pharmacists get this question all the time, and they need the facts to give you useful advice. Have this ready:

- **Which drug and dose** you're on (metronidazole tablets, capsules, or another form) and how many days into the course you are
- **What you drank, how much, and when**
- **When you took your last dose** and when the next one is due
- **Any symptoms** you've had and when they started
- **Your other medicines**, including over-the-counter products and supplements
- **Whether you're pregnant** or have heart, liver, or kidney problems

Most of the time, the answer will be "take your next dose as normal, don't drink again, and call back if you feel unwell." Hearing that from someone who knows your situation is worth the call.

## What About Metronidazole Gel, Cream, or Tinidazole?

**Metronidazole skin gel or cream** (often used for rosacea) is absorbed into the body in very small amounts. An accidental drink while using it is very unlikely to cause a problem, though it's still sensible to follow any advice on your specific product's leaflet.

**Metronidazole vaginal gel** is absorbed more than the skin versions but much less than tablets. The product information still advises avoiding alcohol during use and for a short time afterward. If you drank while using it, the same "stop, watch, call if unsure" approach applies, and a significant reaction would be unlikely.

**Tinidazole** is a close relative of metronidazole that carries a similar alcohol warning, with a longer recommended wait after the last dose (the label says three days). If you're on tinidazole and drank by accident, follow the same steps on this page and ask your pharmacist about timing.

Most other common antibiotics, such as amoxicillin, don't have a specific reaction with alcohol, though drinking while you're sick is still not ideal. Our [antibiotics and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) explains which ones do and don't carry a real warning.

## Getting Through the Rest of Your Course Without Another Slip

Accidental drinks usually happen at social events, when someone hands you a glass, or when you forget a course is still running. A few small habits help:

- **Count the end date.** Work out your last dose, add three days, and put "alcohol OK from" in your phone calendar.
- **Have an easy line ready.** "I'm on antibiotics" is the one excuse almost nobody argues with.
- **Order a drink that looks like a drink.** Soda water with lime or a mocktail stops people offering you refills.
- **Check labels at home.** Swap to an alcohol-free mouthwash and check any liquid medicines for alcohol before you use them.
- **Set a dose reminder.** Missed doses are a bigger threat to your treatment than one accidental drink.

The course usually lasts somewhere between a single dose and two weeks. A short pause is a small price for clearing the infection the first time.

## A Note on DHM and Hangover Supplements Right Now

If you're searching this, you might also be wondering whether a hangover supplement could help. Be careful here.

**There is no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin) or any other supplement prevents or treats a metronidazole-alcohol reaction.** Don't take a supplement as a fix for this situation, and don't use one as a reason to keep drinking. While you're on an antibiotic, it's best not to add new supplements without checking with your pharmacist, simply because it adds another unknown at a time when you're already feeling unwell and taking a prescription drug.

Once your course is finished and the 72 hours have passed, it's a different story. If you get bad hangovers after normal social drinking, DHM is one of the better-studied hangover supplements. Most of its research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and it works best alongside the basics: pacing, food, and water. If you want to try it later, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- An accidental drink on metronidazole usually causes no reaction, or a mild one that passes within a few hours.
- Stop drinking, hydrate, rest, and don't drive.
- **Don't skip your next dose** or stop the course. Take it at the usual time unless a pharmacist or doctor tells you otherwise.
- Get emergency care for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, a severe worsening headache, or vomiting that won't stop.
- Call your doctor or pharmacist if you're pregnant, have a heart condition, or take warfarin, lithium, or disulfiram.
- Avoid alcohol for the rest of the course and for at least 72 hours after your last pill, including alcohol-based mouthwash and liquid medicines.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**I accidentally drank alcohol while taking metronidazole. What should I do?**

Stop drinking, sip water, rest, and don't drive. Take your next dose at the usual time rather than skipping it. Watch for symptoms such as flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, or a racing heart over the next few hours. Most people have no reaction or a mild one that passes. Call your pharmacist or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) for advice, and get emergency care for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or vomiting you can't stop.

**How long after drinking on metronidazole would a reaction start?**

Reactions of this type tend to start fairly soon after drinking, often within minutes to an hour or so, and usually fade over several hours as the alcohol clears. If several hours have passed and you feel normal, a significant reaction is much less likely. Keep an eye on yourself for the rest of the day, especially if you had more than one drink.

**Should I skip my next metronidazole dose after drinking?**

No. Skipping a dose doesn't make it safe to drink, because the drug stays in your body for many hours, and gaps in treatment can let the infection hang on or come back. Take your next dose at the normal time unless a doctor or pharmacist tells you otherwise, and avoid alcohol until 72 hours after your final dose.

**Does drinking alcohol make metronidazole less effective?**

There is no good evidence that a drink stops metronidazole from working against the infection. The bigger risks to your treatment are missed doses and losing a dose through vomiting. If you vomited soon after taking a pill, call your pharmacist to ask whether to repeat it. If your infection symptoms haven't improved by the end of the course, tell your doctor.

**I only had one drink on metronidazole. Will I be okay?**

Most likely, yes. One drink is the most common accidental exposure, and many people notice nothing at all. Stop there, drink water, and watch for symptoms over the next few hours. If you're pregnant, have a heart condition, or take a blood thinner, lithium, or disulfiram, call your doctor or pharmacist to let them know.

**What are the emergency signs after drinking on metronidazole?**

Call 911 or go to the emergency room for chest pain or tightness, a very fast or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, trouble breathing, fainting or nearly fainting, confusion or being hard to wake, vomiting that won't stop or contains blood, a severe headache that keeps getting worse, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat.

**I used alcohol-based mouthwash while on metronidazole. Is that a problem?**

It's unlikely to cause a reaction, because you absorb only a small amount when you rinse and spit. The official advice is still to avoid alcohol-containing products during treatment and for three days after, so switch to an alcohol-free mouthwash for the rest of the course and check liquid medicines for alcohol on the label.

**When can I drink again after an accidental drink on metronidazole?**

The accidental drink doesn't change the timeline. Finish the whole course as prescribed, then wait at least 72 hours (three full days) after your last dose before drinking alcohol. If you're on tinidazole instead, the label also says to wait three days after the last dose.

**Can DHM or a hangover supplement stop a metronidazole reaction?**

There is no good evidence that DHM or any supplement prevents or treats a reaction between metronidazole and alcohol. Don't use one as a fix or as a reason to keep drinking, and check with your pharmacist before adding new supplements while you're on an antibiotic. After you've finished the course and waited 72 hours, DHM is an option some people use for ordinary hangovers.
